note: Thresholds and trajectory choices for engine/visibility.js. Each value names its source in reference/. Values marked provisional have no outside source; the backtest is their only check.

sources.screeningHeightM: Provisional, inside the range the literature gives: 7 +/- 1 km (Taylor 1984), 5 km (Bertolin 2020), about 30 km in older work. See reference/topics/twilight-definitions-and-earth-shadow.md. No value for rocket plumes was found.
sources.maxSunElevationDeg: The twilight phenomenon needs the observer in darkness and the plume in sunlight. See reference/topics/twilight-phenomenon-space-jellyfish.md. No source gives a Sun depression limit, so the limit is the horizon.
sources.minElevationDeg: Provisional. No source found. It stands for trees, buildings, and haze near the horizon.
sources.minAltitudeM: Stage separation at about 65 km on a 2025-11-22 Starlink flight. See reference/topics/falcon9-ascent-timeline.md. The wide plume belongs to the second-stage burn, which starts after separation.

minVisibleSource: Provisional. No source found. A shorter pass is easy to miss.
primeSunElevationSource: End of civil twilight (USNO, NWS). See reference/topics/twilight-definitions-and-earth-shadow.md. Its use as a quality grade is our interpretation.

east.source: An orbit at or below the pad latitude, or an escape orbit, is flown due east: cos(inclination) = cos(latitude) sin(azimuth). See reference/topics/cape-launch-azimuths-and-inclinations.md.

fan.source: LL2 gives no inclination or azimuth. The fan covers the 37 to 114 degree range quoted for the Cape. See reference/topics/cape-launch-azimuths-and-inclinations.md. A second source gives 35 to 120 degrees. 124 is added because a 43 degree Starlink flight on 2025-11-22 went southeast, and the azimuth relation gives 123.6 degrees for that orbit.
